Notes

Pathophysiology of Ulcer Formation

CORE CONCEPT
Ulcer forms when aggressive factors exceed mucosal defenses.
Notes

Main Mechanisms

Loss of mucosal resistance / protective barrier
Excess acid secretion
H. pylori infection
Drugs impairing mucosal protection (NSAIDs / steroids)
Abnormal / reduced gastric motility
SUMMARY RULE
Ulcer formation = ↑ aggressive acid/peptic factors and/or ↓ mucosal protective barrier. Example: Gastrinoma → excessive gastrin → excessive acid production.

Zollinger–Ellison Syndrome (Gastrinoma)

WHEN TO SUSPECT MCQ
Persistent ulcer symptoms despite maximal appropriate therapy/compliance
Multiple ulcers rather than a single ordinary ulcer
Ulcers in unusual / extensive locations
Serum gastrin > 500 pg/mL is Zollinger–Ellison until proven otherwise
Notes

Pathophysiology

Gastrinoma → excessive gastrin secretion → marked gastric acid secretion → severe / recurrent peptic ulceration.

1. Perforated Peptic Ulcer

Unlike chronic uncomplicated ulcer pain, presents with sudden, severe, acute abdominal pain that may interfere with breathing. Examination: acute abdomen, guarding, rigidity, marked tenderness.

GUARDING VS. RIGIDITY VERY IMPORTANT
Guarding: muscles resist palpation, but the abdominal wall can still be partly depressed; resistance may vary. Rigidity: board-like, involuntary contraction; abdomen cannot be depressed.
  • Arthritis patient (NSAIDs) with acute abdominal pain and pneumoperitoneum → perforated peptic ulcer. 442 ×6

IMPORTANT

Any critically ill ER patient (bleeding, trauma, coma, shock, perforation) starts with ABCDE / ABC resuscitation, not disease-specific treatment.

Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Syndrome

Anatomy

Abdominal aorta gives off the celiac trunk, then inferiorly the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). The 3rd part of duodenum passes between the aorta (posteriorly) and the SMA (anteriorly).

Notes

Pathophysiology

Loss of the normal mesenteric fat pad → ↓ angle/distance between aorta and SMA → compression of D3 → SMA syndrome.

CT DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA
Normal aortomesenteric angle ≈ 28.5–60°
Suggestive of SMA syndrome: angle <22° and aortomesenteric distance <8 mm, confirmed on CT imaging.

Stomach and Duodenum

STOMACH: ANATOMY, BLOOD SUPPLY, AND NERVE SUPPLY
1. Functions of the Stomach
The stomach receives food from the esophagus and performs four key functions:

1. Reservoir Function – Allows food intake at intervals by storing boluses of food.

2. Food Mixing & Delivery – Regulates food release into the duodenum based on its chemical nature & texture.

3. Initiation of Digestion – Begins the breakdown of proteins and carbohydrates.

4. Absorption – Facilitates the absorption of small molecules across the gastric mucosa.

2. Anatomy of the Stomach

The stomach is divided into distinct regions based on function and histological cell types:

A. Stomach Regions

1. Cardia – The region near the gastroesophageal junction.

2. Fundus – The uppermost portion of the stomach, above the gastroesophageal junction.

3. Body – The largest central portion.

4. Pyloric Antrum – Distal part of the stomach leading to the pylorus.

5. Pylorus – The exit of the stomach, connecting to the duodenum.

The division between the body & pyloric antrum is marked by the angular incisure, a notch on the lesser curvature.

B. Histology: Gastric Cell Types
Different stomach regions contain specialized cells:
  • Cardiac Gland Area (near the gastroesophageal junction):
  • Mucus-secreting cells (protects the mucosa).
  • Occasionally parietal cells (acid-secreting).
  • Oxyntic (Parietal) Gland Area (Body & Fundus):
  • Parietal (oxyntic) cells – Secrete HCl and intrinsic factor.
  • Chief cells – Secrete pepsinogen (digests proteins).
  • Pyloric Gland Area (Distal stomach, 30% of stomach length):
  • G-cells – Produce gastrin (stimulates acid secretion).
  • Mucous cells – Secrete protective mucus.
C. Muscular Layers

The stomach wall consists of three muscle layers (unlike the rest of the GI tract, which has only two):

1. Outer longitudinal layer.

2. Middle circular layer.

3. Innermost oblique layer (most prominent near the lesser curvature).

  • Important in gastric cancer metastasis, spreading along gastric lymph nodes.
4. Nerve Supply of the Stomach

The stomach is innervated by both the parasympathetic & sympathetic nervous systems.

A. Parasympathetic Innervation (Vagus Nerve)
  • Primary function: Stimulates acid secretion, motility, and digestion.
  • Vagus nerve trunks pass through the esophageal hiatus:
  • Right vagus nerve → Becomes posterior gastric nerve.
  • Left vagus nerve → Becomes anterior gastric nerve.
  • Vagal branches:

1. Hepatic Branch (from anterior vagus) → Travels to liver via lesser omentum.

2. Celiac Branch (from posterior vagus) → Innervates midgut & hindgut.

3. Nerves of Latarjet → Run along the lesser curvature, supplying distal stomach.

  • Vagal fibers synapse in the Auerbach's Plexus (Myenteric Plexus):
  • Preganglionic vagal fibers synapse in Auerbach’s plexus.
  • Postganglionic fibers stimulate smooth muscle contraction & acid secretion.
B. Sympathetic Innervation (Celiac Plexus)
  • Originates from T6-T9 segments of the spinal cord.
  • Postganglionic fibers follow arterial pathways from the celiac plexus.
  • Functions:
  • Inhibits gastric motility.
  • Reduces acid secretion.
  • Causes vasoconstriction.
Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)
1. Definition and Pathophysiology
  • Peptic ulcers are defects in the gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa caused by the

corrosive action of gastric acid and pepsin.

  • They commonly occur in:
  • Duodenum (most common)
  • Stomach
  • Esophagus
  • Jejunum (after gastrojejunostomy)
  • Meckel’s diverticulum (due to ectopic gastric mucosa)
  • Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection and excessive acid production are the

primary causes.

2. Epidemiology
  • Prevalence: ~2% of the adult U.S. population has active PUD, with a lifetime

risk of 10%.

  • Male-to-Female Ratio: 3:1.
  • Duodenal Ulcers: 10x more common than gastric ulcers in young patients, but

equal in older populations.

  • Declining Incidence: Due to reduced H. pylori infection rates.
3. Clinical Manifestations
A. General Symptoms

1. Epigastric pain – Burning, gnawing, or aching pain.

2. Pain relief with food or antacids (duodenal ulcer).

3. Pain worsened by food intake (gastric ulcer).

4. Nocturnal pain – Waking up at night due to pain.

5. Nausea & vomiting – More common in gastric ulcers.

6. Melena or hematemesis – Due to bleeding ulcers.

B. Complications

1. Hemorrhage – GI bleeding due to ulcer erosion.

2. Perforation – Ulcer penetration through gut wall.

3. Obstruction – Pyloric scarring/swelling.

4. Penetration – Ulcer invading other organs (e.g., pancreas).

4. Diagnosis
A. Endoscopy (Gold Standard)
  • Confirms presence, location, and severity of ulcers.
  • Biopsy: Required for gastric ulcers to rule out malignancy.
  • Tests for H. pylori (urease test, histology, culture).
B. Noninvasive H. Pylori Tests

1. Urea Breath Test (most accurate) 2. Fecal Antigen Test 3. Serology (not useful for active infection)

C. Gastric Acid Analysis
  • Basal Acid Output (BAO) & Maximal Acid Output (MAO) may help detect

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma).

D. Serum Gastrin Levels
  • >200 pg/mL suggests hypergastrinemia.
  • Secretin stimulation test distinguishes Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome

(gastrinoma).

E. Imaging
  • Upper GI series with contrast (for patients unable to undergo endoscopy).
5. Treatment
A. Medical Therapy
1. H. pylori Eradication (if positive)
  • Triple Therapy (14 days):
  • PPI (Omeprazole 20 mg BID or Lansoprazole 30 mg BID)
  • Amoxicillin 1000 mg BID
  • Clarithromycin 500 mg BID (or Metronidazole 500 mg BID if allergic to

penicillin)

  • Quadruple Therapy (if resistant or allergic to macrolides):
  • PPI
  • Bismuth 525 mg QID
  • Tetracycline 500 mg QID
  • Metronidazole 500 mg TID
2. Acid Suppression Therapy
  • Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) (First-line)
  • Omeprazole, Pantoprazole, Lansoprazole
  • Most effective for ulcer healing & preventing recurrence.
  • H2-Receptor Antagonists (e.g., Ranitidine, Famotidine)
  • Less effective than PPIs but used in mild cases.
3. Antacids & Cytoprotective Agents
  • Sucralfate – Protects ulcer base.
  • Misoprostol – Prostaglandin analog, useful in NSAID-induced ulcers.
  • Antacids (e.g., Aluminum Hydroxide, Magnesium Hydroxide) – Provide

symptomatic relief.

B. Surgical Treatment (Indicated for Complications)
Indications for Surgery:

1. Refractory ulcers despite medical therapy.

2. Severe bleeding or perforation.

3. Obstruction due to scarring.

4. Suspicion of malignancy (especially in gastric ulcers).

Surgical Procedures
1. Vagotomy + Drainage Procedure (Pyloroplasty or Gastrojejunostomy)
  • Truncal Vagotomy: Resection of both vagal trunks.
  • Selective Vagotomy: Preserves hepatic and celiac branches.
  • Highly Selective (Parietal Cell) Vagotomy: Preserves antral innervation.

2. Antrectomy + Vagotomy

  • Removes gastrin-producing antral cells.
  • Requires Billroth I or Billroth II reconstruction.

3. Subtotal Gastrectomy

  • Reserved for severe/refractory cases.
6. Complications of Surgery
A. Early Complications

1. Anastomotic Leak – Risk highest at 5–10 days post-op.

2. Postoperative Hemorrhage – Can occur at anastomotic sites.

3. Duodenal Stump Leak – A major complication of Billroth II reconstruction.

4. Gastric Outlet Obstruction – Due to edema/scarring at the anastomosis.

B. Late Complications
1. Recurrent Ulceration (Marginal Ulcer)
  • Occurs in 10% after vagotomy & pyloroplasty.
  • Tx: PPIs or revision surgery.

2. Gastrocolic/Gastrojejunal Fistula

  • Severe diarrhea, weight loss, malnutrition.
  • Tx: Fistula resection and gastric revision surgery.

3. Dumping Syndrome

  • Symptoms:
  • Early Dumping (15-30 min after meals): Palpitations, sweating, dizziness,

diarrhea.

  • Late Dumping (1-3 hours after meals): Hypoglycemia, weakness.
  • Tx: Dietary modifications (low carbs, high protein, small meals).

4. Alkaline Gastritis

  • Chronic reflux of bile into the stomach.
  • Tx: Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy.

5. Anemia

  • Iron Deficiency (30% post-gastrectomy).
  • Vitamin B12 Deficiency due to loss of intrinsic factor.
  • Tx: Iron and lifelong B12 supplementation.

6. Post-Vagotomy Diarrhea

  • Occurs in 5-10% of cases.
  • Tx: Antidiarrheal agents (Loperamide, Codeine).

7. Chronic Gastroparesis

  • Delayed gastric emptying.
  • Tx: Prokinetic agents (Metoclopramide) or total gastrectomy in severe cases.

8. Late Duodenal Stump Leak

  • Can occur years after Billroth II reconstruction.
  • Tx: Endoscopic drainage or exploratory laparotomy.
7. Prevention of Peptic Ulcer Disease
  • H. pylori Eradication – Prevents recurrence.
  • Avoid NSAIDs – If necessary, co-prescribe PPIs or Misoprostol.
  • Smoking & Alcohol Cessation – Reduces ulcer risk.
  • Dietary Modifications – Reduce acid-stimulating foods.
Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (Gastrinoma)
1. Definition
  • Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) is a rare condition characterized by gastric

acid hypersecretion due to a gastrin-producing neuroendocrine tumor (Gastrinoma).

  • The tumor primarily occurs in the duodenum (most common site), pancreas,

and rarely in the liver or ovaries.

  • Key Features:
  • Severe peptic ulcer disease (95% of cases).
  • Hypergastrinemia with gastric acid hypersecretion.
  • Associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN 1) in ~30% of

cases.

  • High recurrence and metastatic potential (malignant in ~60-90%).
2. Epidemiology
  • Incidence: 1-3 cases per million per year.
  • Median age of diagnosis: 40-50 years.
  • Gender: More common in males.
  • Associated with MEN 1 (parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreatic tumors).
3. Pathophysiology
  • Gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) → Stimulates excessive acid production

(hyperchlorhydria).

  • Effects of Hypergastrinemia:

1. Increased gastric acid secretion → Multiple severe ulcers (refractory to treatment).

2. Hypertrophy of gastric mucosa (thickened gastric folds).

3. Inactivation of pancreatic enzymes → Steatorrhea & malabsorption.

4. Diarrhea from excessive gastric secretion and mucosal damage.

4. Clinical Manifestations
A. Symptoms

1. Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) – Often multiple & recurrent.

2. Severe epigastric pain – Poor response to standard ulcer therapy.

3. Diarrhea & steatorrhea – Due to inactivation of pancreatic enzymes by excess acid.

4. Nausea & vomiting.

5. Weight loss.

6. Gastrointestinal bleeding – Ulcers may cause melena or hematemesis.

7. Complications:

  • Perforation.
  • Obstruction (due to inflammation or scarring).
  • Marginal ulcers after surgery.
5. Diagnosis
A. Laboratory Tests
1. Serum Gastrin Levels (First-line test)
  • Normal: < 200 pg/mL.
  • ZES likely: > 1000 pg/mL.
  • Borderline (200-500 pg/mL) → Perform secretin stimulation test.
2. Secretin Stimulation Test (Confirmatory)
  • Secretin (2 units/kg IV) → Rise in gastrin > 150 pg/mL within 15 min is

diagnostic.

  • Highly specific for ZES.

3. Gastric Acid Analysis

  • Basal Acid Output (BAO) > 15 mEq/h (intact stomach) or > 5 mEq/h (post-

surgical patients).

  • BAO/MAO (maximal acid output) ratio > 0.6 suggests gastrinoma.

4. Calcium & PTH Levels

  • Elevated in MEN 1 patients (parathyroid involvement).

5. Chromogranin-A & Neuron-Specific Enolase

  • Markers for neuroendocrine tumors (NETs).
B. Imaging Studies
1. CT Scan or MRI
  • Detects pancreatic or metastatic gastrinomas.
  • Best for large tumors.

2. Somatostatin Receptor Scintigraphy (SRS)

  • Most sensitive test (90% detection rate).
  • Uses labeled octreotide to detect somatostatin receptors on tumor cells.

3. Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)

  • Best for detecting small tumors (< 2 cm) in the pancreas or duodenum.

4. Selective Arterial Secretin Injection (Rarely Used)

  • Identifies tumors by measuring gastrin levels in hepatic venous blood after

arterial secretin injection.

5. Upper GI Series with Barium

  • May show ulcers in distal duodenum or jejunum (strong indicator of ZES).
6. Treatment
A. Medical Management
1. Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) – First-line
  • Omeprazole 40 mg BID (adjusted to keep gastric acid output < 5 mEq/h).
  • Alternative: Lansoprazole, Esomeprazole, Pantoprazole.
2. H2-Receptor Antagonists (Less Effective)
  • Ranitidine (300-450 mg/day) or Famotidine (40-80 mg/day).

3. Somatostatin Analogs (Octreotide)

  • Suppresses gastrin secretion.
  • Used for metastatic disease or MEN 1 patients.
B. Surgical Treatment (Curative in Localized Disease)
  • Indications for Surgery:

1. Localized, resectable gastrinoma.

2. No evidence of metastases.

3. Patient has sporadic (non-MEN 1) disease.

  • Procedure:
  • Enucleation of duodenal or pancreatic tumors.
  • Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) for larger tumors.
  • Gastrinoma Triangle:
  • 90% of tumors are found within the area between the duodenum, pancreatic

neck, and cystic/common bile duct.

  • Intraoperative ultrasound & duodenotomy improve detection.
C. Management of Metastatic Disease
  • Liver metastases: Surgical debulking or hepatic artery embolization.
  • Somatostatin receptor analogs (Octreotide) – Control symptoms.
  • Targeted therapies (e.g., Everolimus, Sunitinib) – Used in progressive or

unresectable tumors.

  • Chemotherapy – Used in advanced, metastatic cases (Streptozocin +

Doxorubicin).

7. Prognosis
  • Localized gastrinomas:
  • 70% cure rate after resection.
  • 30% remain disease-free at 5 years.
  • Metastatic disease:
  • Liver metastases worsen prognosis (median survival 5-10 years).
  • MEN 1-associated ZES:
  • Surgical cure unlikely due to multiple tumors.
  • Lifelong PPI therapy required.
Gastric Ulcer
1. Definition
  • Gastric ulcers are mucosal defects in the stomach caused by the corrosive

action of gastric acid and pepsin.

  • Unlike duodenal ulcers, gastric ulcers are more common in older patients (40-

60 years).

  • Associated Conditions:
  • H. pylori infection (major cause).
  • NSAID or corticosteroid use.
  • Gastric acid hypersecretion (e.g., Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome).
  • Gastric cancer (malignant ulcers must be ruled out).
2. Epidemiology
  • Peak incidence: 40-60 years (older than duodenal ulcer patients).
  • Gender: More common in men.
  • Common Location: 95% occur along the lesser curvature of the stomach.
  • Complications: Bleeding, perforation, gastric outlet obstruction.

4. Pathophysiology
  • H. pylori Infection (most common cause)
  • Disrupts mucosal defense, allowing acid-induced injury.
  • Produces urease, increasing gastric pH, leading to inflammatory damage.
  • NSAID-Induced Ulcers:
  • Inhibit prostaglandins, reducing gastric mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
  • Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome:
  • Gastrin-producing tumor → Excess acid → Refractory ulcers.
  • Stress-Related Ulcers:
  • Critically ill patients (ICU, burns, sepsis).
  • Common in mechanical ventilation.
5. Clinical Features
A. Symptoms
1. Epigastric pain (burning/gnawing)
  • Worse with eating (postprandial pain within 30 minutes).
  • Relieved by fasting (opposite of duodenal ulcers).

2. Nausea & vomiting.

3. Weight loss & anorexia (more common than in duodenal ulcers).

4. Gastrointestinal bleeding (hematemesis, melena).

5. Gastric outlet obstruction (due to inflammation and scarring).

6. Perforation → Acute peritonitis, sudden severe pain.

B. Physical Examination
  • Epigastric tenderness (localized to mid-upper abdomen).
  • Anemia (chronic blood loss) → Pallor, fatigue.
  • Signs of perforation → Board-like rigidity, rebound tenderness.
6. Diagnosis
A. Endoscopy (Gold Standard)
  • Direct visualization of ulcer.
  • Biopsy for malignancy (especially in non-healing ulcers).
  • Findings Suggestive of Malignancy:
  • Irregular, thickened margins.
  • Nodular or ulcerated mass.
  • Fold fusion around ulcer crater.
B. H. pylori Testing
1. Biopsy-based tests (endoscopic)
  • Urease test (rapid, detects bacterial urease).
  • Histology (Gold standard for confirming H. pylori).

2. Non-invasive tests:

  • Urea breath test (most accurate non-invasive test).
  • Stool antigen test.
  • Serology (not recommended for active infection detection).
C. Gastric Acid Analysis
  • Basal acid output (BAO) and maximal acid output (MAO).
  • Elevated gastrin levels → Suggest Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome.
D. Imaging Studies
  • Barium X-ray (less commonly used today).
  • Suggests malignancy if:
  • Ulcer extends beyond expected gastric wall border.
  • Irregular, heaped-up edges.
  • CT scan: Evaluates for perforation, metastases.
7. Differential Diagnosis
  • Duodenal ulcer: Pain relieved by food (gastric ulcer pain worsens with food).
  • Gastric cancer: Weight loss, early satiety, biopsy needed.
  • GERD: Acid reflux symptoms, endoscopy differentiation.
  • Chronic pancreatitis: Epigastric pain radiating to back, enzyme deficiencies.

9. Treatment
A. Medical Management (First-line)
1. Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) – Gold Standard
  • Omeprazole 20-40 mg daily (or equivalent: Lansoprazole, Pantoprazole).
  • Duration: 6-8 weeks (repeat endoscopy for healing assessment).

2. H. pylori Eradication (if positive) – Triple or Quadruple Therapy

  • Triple Therapy (First-line):
  • PPI + Clarithromycin + Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole if penicillin allergy) for

14 days.

  • Quadruple Therapy (if resistant or failed initial therapy):
  • PPI + Bismuth + Tetracycline + Metronidazole.

3. Discontinue NSAIDs / Smoking Cessation

  • NSAID-induced ulcers: Stop NSAIDs and give PPI + misoprostol or sucralfate.

4. Repeat Endoscopy (after 8-12 weeks)

  • Required for all gastric ulcers to confirm healing.
  • Persistent ulcers → Biopsy for malignancy.
B. Surgical Treatment (For Complications)
  • Indications for Surgery:
  • Failure of medical therapy.
  • Complications (bleeding, perforation, obstruction).
  • Suspicion of malignancy.

  • For high acid-secreting ulcers (Type II & III).

2. Subtotal Gastrectomy (Distal Hemigastrectomy)

  • For Type I & IV ulcers or suspected malignancy.
  • Reconstruction:
  • Billroth I (Gastroduodenostomy) – Preferred.
  • Billroth II (Gastrojejunostomy) – Used in some cases.

3. Total Gastrectomy:

  • For gastric cancer.
10. Prognosis
  • Most ulcers heal with medical therapy (PPI + H. pylori eradication).
  • Persistent ulcers require repeat endoscopy to rule out malignancy.
  • NSAID-induced ulcers have a high recurrence rate if NSAIDs are continued.
Upper Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage
1. Definition
  • Upper gastrointestinal (GI) hemorrhage refers to bleeding originating

proximal to the ligament of Treitz (esophagus, stomach, duodenum).

  • Most Common Causes:
  • Peptic ulcer disease (gastric or duodenal ulcers) – 50% of cases.
  • Esophageal varices (portal hypertension).
  • Gastritis, duodenitis, or esophagitis.
  • Mallory-Weiss tears (mucosal lacerations at gastroesophageal junction).
  • Gastric malignancy (gastric adenocarcinoma).
  • Vascular malformations (Dieulafoy’s lesion, AV malformations).
2. Clinical Presentation
A. Symptoms
1. Hematemesis (vomiting of blood)
  • Bright red blood = Active, severe bleeding.
  • Coffee-ground emesis = Slower bleeding, blood digested by gastric acid.

2. Melena (black, tarry stools)

  • Indicates digested blood from prolonged upper GI bleeding.

3. Hematochezia (passage of bright red blood per rectum)

  • Usually lower GI bleeding, but can occur in massive upper GI bleeding with

rapid transit.

4. Other Symptoms

  • Epigastric pain (suggests peptic ulcer disease).
  • Dysphagia, odynophagia (suggests esophagitis or malignancy).
  • Jaundice, ascites, hepatosplenomegaly (suggests variceal bleeding from liver

disease).

  • Syncope, dizziness, shock (suggests severe bleeding).
B. Signs of Hypovolemia/Shock
  • Tachycardia (HR > 100 bpm)
  • Hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg)
  • Orthostatic changes
  • Cold, clammy skin
  • Oliguria or anuria
  • Altered mental status
3. Diagnosis
A. Initial Assessment & Laboratory Workup
  • Hemoglobin & Hematocrit (initial values may be normal due to

hemoconcentration; repeat serially).

  • Blood type & crossmatch (prepare for transfusion).
  • Coagulation profile (PT, INR, aPTT for liver disease or anticoagulation use).
  • BUN/Creatinine Ratio (BUN:Cr > 30 suggests upper GI bleeding due to

digestion of blood).

  • Liver function tests (AST, ALT, ALP, bilirubin) (assess for liver disease).
  • Nasogastric (NG) Tube Lavage (confirms active bleeding if bloody aspirate is

present).

B. Endoscopy (Gold Standard)
  • Upper endoscopy (EGD) within 24 hours is the preferred method for

identifying the source of bleeding.

  • Can be diagnostic and therapeutic (allows for hemostatic interventions).
C. Imaging & Other Studies
  • CT Angiography (used for ongoing bleeding when endoscopy is inconclusive).
  • Selective Angiography (used in active bleeding cases; allows for

embolization).

  • Labeled RBC Scintigraphy (used when the bleeding source is unidentified but

ongoing).

  • Large ulcer size (> 2 cm).
  • Rebleeding after initial stabilization.
  • Coagulopathy (elevated INR).
  • Comorbid conditions (cardiovascular, renal failure).
B. Risk of Rebleeding
  • Rebleeding occurs in ~25% of patients.

Hemorrhage from Peptic Ulcer
1. Overview
  • Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) accounts for 50% of massive upper gastrointestinal

(GI) hemorrhage cases.

  • 20% of PUD patients experience bleeding, which contributes to 40% of peptic

ulcer-related deaths.

  • Gastric and duodenal ulcers have a similar risk of bleeding, but gastric ulcers

tend to cause more severe hemorrhage.

2. Pathophysiology
  • Duodenal Ulcers:
  • Most bleeding ulcers are posterior ulcers in the duodenal bulb.
  • As the ulcer penetrates, it erodes the gastroduodenal artery, causing

significant bleeding.

  • Anterior ulcers are more likely to perforate rather than bleed.
  • Postbulbar ulcers (located in the second part of the duodenum) can also bleed

but are less common.

  • Gastric Ulcers:
  • Most located on the lesser curvature of the stomach.
  • Can erode into large arteries, causing massive hemorrhage.
  • More likely to rebleed than duodenal ulcers (30% vs. 10% rebleeding rate).
3. Clinical Presentation
A. Symptoms

1. Hematemesis (vomiting of bright red blood or coffee-ground emesis).

2. Melena (black, tarry stools due to digested blood).

3. Hematochezia (bright red blood in stool, seen in massive bleeding).

4. Shock symptoms:

  • Hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg).
  • Tachycardia (HR > 100 bpm).
  • Cold, clammy skin.
  • Altered mental status (severe cases).
B. Risk Factors for Severe Bleeding & Rebleeding
  • Age > 60 years.
  • Hematocrit < 30% or Hemoglobin < 8 g/dL on admission.
  • Active bleeding during endoscopy.
  • Large ulcers (>2 cm).
  • Presence of visible blood vessel in ulcer base.
  • Hypotension or shock at presentation.
  • Need for multiple blood transfusions.
4. Diagnosis
A. Laboratory Tests
  • Complete Blood Count (CBC): Low hemoglobin and hematocrit.
  • Blood Type & Crossmatch: Prepare for transfusion.
  • Coagulation Profile (INR, PT, aPTT): Evaluate for coagulopathy.
  • Liver Function Tests: Assess for cirrhosis (if variceal bleeding is suspected).
  • BUN/Creatinine Ratio (> 30): Suggests upper GI bleeding due to digested

blood.

B. Imaging & Endoscopy
  • Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) (Gold Standard)
  • Should be done within 24 hours of admission.
  • Identifies the source of bleeding and allows for therapeutic intervention.
  • Findings Predicting Rebleeding:
  • Active bleeding at time of endoscopy.
  • Visible vessel in ulcer base.
  • Adherent clot.
  • Large ulcer (>2 cm).
  • CT Angiography (if endoscopy is inconclusive or bleeding persists).
  • Angiography with embolization (for persistent bleeding not controlled by

endoscopy).

  • Place two large-bore IV lines (18G or larger).
  • Initiate IV fluid resuscitation (Normal Saline or Lactated Ringer’s).
  • Blood transfusion if needed (target Hgb > 7 g/dL).
  • Reverse anticoagulation if applicable (e.g., Vitamin K & FFP for warfarin users).
  • Start IV Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) Therapy:
  • Pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus → 8 mg/hr infusion.
  • Reduces acid secretion and promotes clot stability.

Billroth II or Roux-en-Y GastrojejunostomyIf ulcer involves posterior wall of the duodenal bulb
  • Preferred approach: Minimal intervention in unstable patients (oversewing

only) and definitive ulcer management (vagotomy + pyloroplasty) in stable patients.

7. Prognosis & Mortality
A. Rebleeding & Mortality Rates
  • 30% rebleeding rate for gastric ulcers, 10% for duodenal ulcers.
  • Rebleeding significantly increases mortality risk (~30% death rate if

rebleeding occurs).

  • Overall mortality for massive GI bleeding: 10-15%.
B. Predictors of Poor Outcome
  • Age > 60 years.
  • Shock on admission (SBP < 90 mmHg, HR > 100 bpm).
  • Hemoglobin < 8 g/dL on presentation.
  • Active bleeding at endoscopy.
  • Recurrent bleeding despite initial control.
  • Coagulopathy (INR > 1.5).
Mallory-Weiss Syndrome
1. Overview
  • Mallory-Weiss syndrome (MWS) accounts for 10% of acute upper

gastrointestinal (GI) hemorrhage cases.

  • The condition is characterized by longitudinal mucosal tears near the

gastroesophageal junction.

  • The tear typically does not extend into the muscularis mucosae.
  • It is often precipitated by forceful retching, vomiting, or increased intra-

abdominal pressure.

2. Pathophysiology
  • The mucosal tear results from a sudden increase in intra-abdominal and

intragastric pressure.

  • This is commonly triggered by:
  • Forceful vomiting or retching.
  • Alcohol abuse (most common cause).
  • Hiatal hernia (found in ~66% of cases).
  • Severe coughing.
  • Seizures.
  • Childbirth or weightlifting.
  • Closed-chest cardiac compressions (rare cases).
  • Tear Location:
  • 75% are confined to the stomach.
  • 20% cross the gastroesophageal junction.
  • 5% occur entirely in the distal esophagus.
3. Clinical Presentation
A. Symptoms
  • Classic Triad:

1. Initial vomiting of gastric contents.

2. Forceful retching.

3. Hematemesis (vomiting of bright red blood or coffee-ground material).

  • Additional symptoms:
  • Melena (black, tarry stools in some cases).
  • Epigastric pain or discomfort.
  • Syncope in severe blood loss.
B. Risk Factors
  • Alcoholism (most common).
  • Bulimia nervosa or eating disorders.
  • Hiatal hernia.
  • Severe gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
  • Straining (e.g., childbirth, weightlifting, seizures).
4. Diagnosis
A. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) – Gold Standard
  • Findings:
  • 1–4 cm longitudinal mucosal tear near the gastroesophageal junction.
  • Actively bleeding tear or evidence of recent bleeding.
  • Presence of hiatal hernia (common).
B. Laboratory Tests
  • Complete Blood Count (CBC): Evaluates blood loss (low

hemoglobin/hematocrit).

  • Coagulation Profile (INR, PT, aPTT): Assesses for coagulopathy.
  • Liver Function Tests: Assesses for alcoholic liver disease, which increases

bleeding risk.

C. Imaging
  • CT Angiography (only if bleeding source is unclear).
  • Nasogastric Lavage:
  • Bright red blood confirms upper GI bleeding.
  • Coffee-ground material suggests older bleeding.
5. Treatment & Management
A. Initial Management
  • Assess ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation).
  • Place two large-bore IV lines (18G or larger).
  • Resuscitation with IV fluids (normal saline or lactated Ringer’s).
  • Blood transfusion if Hgb < 7 g/dL.
  • Correct coagulopathy (Vitamin K & FFP for anticoagulated patients).
  • Start IV Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI):
  • Pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus → 8 mg/hr infusion.
B. Endoscopic Therapy (First-line)
  • Most cases (90%) stop bleeding spontaneously.
  • If active bleeding persists, endoscopic intervention is performed:
Endoscopic MethodMechanism
Electrocautery (heater probe)Coagulates bleeding vessels
Hemostatic ClipsMechanically closes the tear
Epinephrine InjectionInduces vasoconstriction to reduce bleeding
Banding (if varices present)Controls associated esophageal varices
C. Angiographic Embolization (Second-line)
  • Used if endoscopic therapy fails.
  • Procedure:
  • Selective embolization of bleeding vessels with Gelfoam, coils, or

microspheres.

D. Surgery (Rare, Last Resort)
  • Indications for Surgery:
  • Persistent bleeding despite endoscopic & angiographic intervention.
  • Refractory bleeding in hemodynamically unstable patients.
  • Surgical Procedure:
  • Gastrotomy with oversewing of the tear.
  • Absorbable sutures used to close mucosal defects.
  • Postoperative recurrence is rare.
6. Prognosis & Complications
  • Prognosis:
  • Excellent prognosis with conservative management.
  • 90% of cases resolve spontaneously.
  • Rebleeding is uncommon after successful treatment.
  • Potential Complications:
  • Massive hemorrhage (uncommon but can be life-threatening).
  • Boerhaave Syndrome (esophageal rupture due to severe vomiting).
  • Aspiration pneumonia (from swallowed blood).
  • Recurrent bleeding (rare).
Perforated Peptic Ulcer
1. Overview
  • Perforation is a serious complication of peptic ulcer disease (PUD), occurring

half as often as hemorrhage.

  • Most perforations occur in the anterior wall of the duodenum or stomach,

leading to leakage of gastric contents into the peritoneal cavity.

  • Mortality rate is 15%, with increased risk in elderly patients, females, and

gastric ulcers.

2. Pathophysiology
  • Anterior ulcers → Tend to perforate because of lack of protective structures

(viscera, blood vessels).

  • Posterior ulcers → More likely to bleed as they are close to major blood

vessels (e.g., gastroduodenal artery).

  • Immediate consequences:
  • Chemical peritonitis due to gastric acid, bile, and pancreatic enzymes.
  • Sterile peritonitis (initial 12-24 hrs) → Becomes bacterial peritonitis if

untreated.

  • Risk of abscess formation if the perforation becomes sealed by adjacent

structures (e.g., liver).

  • High-risk cases:
  • Delayed treatment > 12-24 hours.
  • Elderly patients.
  • Patients with underlying medical conditions.
3. Clinical Presentation
A. Symptoms
  • Sudden, severe epigastric pain (“knife-like” pain).
  • Pain radiates to the right shoulder (if diaphragm irritation occurs).
  • Onset often recalled precisely by the patient.
  • No nausea or vomiting (unlike other GI conditions).
  • Pain temporarily improves before bacterial peritonitis develops.
  • Shock (in severe cases).
B. Physical Examination
  • Patient appears distressed, lying still with knees drawn up.
  • Shallow breathing to reduce abdominal motion.
  • Board-like rigidity due to involuntary abdominal muscle spasm.
  • Absent or reduced bowel sounds (due to paralytic ileus).
  • Loss of liver dullness on percussion (air under diaphragm).
  • Tympany over liver instead of dullness (if free air is present).
C. Atypical Presentations
  • Mild peritonitis in small perforations.
  • Right lower quadrant pain (may mimic appendicitis if leakage is localized).
  • Less dramatic findings in elderly, immunocompromised, or hospitalized

patients.

4. Diagnosis
A. Laboratory Findings
  • Leukocytosis (WBC 12,000–20,000/µL).
  • Elevated serum amylase (mild, from duodenal contents in peritoneal cavity).
  • Mild metabolic acidosis (due to shock or sepsis).
  • Lactic acidosis (if septic peritonitis develops).
B. Imaging Studies
X-ray (First-line)
  • Findings: Free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) in 85% of cases.
  • If no free air is seen → Proceed to CT scan.
CT Abdomen with Contrast (Gold Standard)
  • Findings: Air outside the GI tract, fluid collection, and site of perforation.
Water-Soluble Contrast Study (If needed)
  • Use if CT is unavailable or inconclusive.
  • Findings: Extravasation of contrast confirms perforation.

6. Management & Treatment
A. Initial Resuscitation (Critical Step)
Immediate Actions:

1. NPO (Nothing by mouth).

2. Insert nasogastric (NG) tube (to decompress stomach).

3. IV fluids (aggressive resuscitation with normal saline or lactated Ringer’s).

4. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics:

  • Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole or Piperacillin-Tazobactam.

5. IV Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI):

  • Pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus → 8 mg/hr continuous infusion.

6. Pain control (IV opioids like fentanyl or morphine).

7. Monitor for signs of shock (tachycardia, hypotension).

B. Definitive Surgical Management
  • Laparoscopic Closure (Gold Standard)
  • Preferred method for most cases.
  • Omental patch repair (Graham-Steele patch).
  • Gastric ulcers require biopsy to rule out malignancy.
  • Laparotomy (Open Surgery)
  • Indicated if:
  • Large perforation (> 2 cm).
  • Severe peritonitis.
  • Hemodynamic instability.
  • Steps: 1. Closure of perforation (suture + omental patch). 2. Irrigation of peritoneal cavity (remove contamination). 3. Drain placement (if needed for ongoing leakage monitoring).
C. Non-Surgical (Conservative) Management
  • ONLY for high-risk patients (elderly, unstable, high surgical risk).
  • Requires close monitoring and aggressive medical therapy:
  • Nasogastric suction.
  • IV antibiotics & PPIs.
  • Serial abdominal exams & imaging.
  • Failure to improve = Immediate surgery.
7. Postoperative & Long-Term Management
A. Postoperative Care
  • Continue IV antibiotics for 3-5 days.
  • Gradual diet advancement (NPO → clear liquids → soft diet).
  • Monitor for complications (abscess, sepsis, ileus, re-perforation).
  • Serial abdominal imaging (if needed for delayed complications).
B. H. pylori Eradication Therapy
Triple Therapy (First-line):
  • PPI + Amoxicillin + Clarithromycin (14 days). ✔ Quadruple Therapy (If
resistant or prior failure):
  • PPI + Bismuth + Tetracycline + Metronidazole.
C. Long-Term Acid Suppression
  • Continue PPIs for at least 6-8 weeks.
  • Avoid NSAIDs or corticosteroids if possible.
  • Regular endoscopic surveillance if gastric ulcer present.
8. Prognosis & Complications
A. Prognosis
  • Mortality ~15% (higher in elderly or delayed treatment).
  • Better survival if surgery is performed within 6-12 hours.
  • Excellent prognosis with early intervention.
B. Complications
  • Sepsis & Septic Shock (if peritonitis worsens).
  • Intra-abdominal abscess (if untreated).
  • Fistula formation (rare).
  • Recurrent ulcer if H. pylori is not treated.
Stress Ulcers
1. Overview
  • Stress ulcers refer to acute gastric or duodenal ulcers that develop secondary

to physiological stress.

  • Common causes include: 1. Shock 2. Sepsis 3. Burns (Curling ulcers) 4. CNS injury (Cushing ulcers)
  • Key complications: Gastrointestinal bleeding (most common) and perforation (in ~10% of cases).
  • Typically occur within 72 hours after a stressful event.
2. Pathophysiology
  • Decreased mucosal resistance due to ischemia and toxins.
  • Impaired gastric mucosal blood flow → Reduced bicarbonate buffer supply.
  • Impaired mucosal repair (↓ prostaglandins, ↓ mucosal renewal).
  • Superoxide and hydroxyl radicals contribute to mucosal damage.
  • Platelet-activating factor (PAF) & endotoxin play a role in septic ulcers.
  • Acid hypersecretion contributes in burn patients but is not the primary cause.
3. Clinical Features
A. Symptoms
  • Often asymptomatic unless complications arise.
  • Epigastric pain (mild, non-specific).
  • Hematemesis & Melena (if ulcer erodes a blood vessel).
  • Massive GI bleeding may occur 4-5 days after the initial injury.
B. Endoscopic Findings
  • Shallow, discrete gastric erosions.
  • Mild congestion & edema, minimal inflammation.
  • Occurs primarily in the stomach, sometimes in the duodenum.
  • Bleeding sites commonly seen after 3-5 days.
4. Diagnosis
  • Upper endoscopy (Gold Standard) → Identifies erosions, ulcers, and active

bleeding.

  • Laboratory tests:
  • Hematocrit & hemoglobin (to assess blood loss).
  • Lactate levels (indicate ischemia in critically ill patients).
  • Coagulation studies (to rule out coagulopathy-related bleeding).
  • CT Abdomen (if perforation is suspected).
5. Prevention & Treatment
A. Prevention (Key Strategy)
  • Initiate stress ulcer prophylaxis in high-risk patients:
  • IV Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPI)
  • Pantoprazole 40 mg IV BID or
  • Omeprazole 40 mg daily. H2-Receptor Blockers (alternative for mild cases). Enteral feeding → Enhances mucosal protection.
B. Treatment
1. Medical Therapy
PPI therapy (first-line)
  • IV Pantoprazole 80 mg bolus → Continuous infusion (8 mg/hr).
